name: Zeigarnik effect
statement: Interrupted tasks are said to be recalled better than completed ones, because an unfinished intention leaves a tension that keeps it live in memory.
meaning: Kurt Lewin's field theory held that taking on a task sets up a quasi-need, a state of tension that discharges when the task is done. Zeigarnik's prediction followed from it. If the tension survives interruption, the unfinished task should stay available for recall. The test is the interrupted task paradigm: a run of short tasks, half of them stopped part-way through, followed by an unannounced request to list what the participant worked on. The score is usually the ratio of interrupted tasks recalled to completed tasks recalled, written IR/CR, where 1.0 means no difference. Zeigarnik reported a ratio near 2. Popular writing takes the same idea much further, using it to explain cliffhangers, unread notifications and the pull of an unfinished to-do list.

origin.who: Bluma Zeigarnik, working under Kurt Lewin
origin.note: Zeigarnik ran the experiments in Berlin between 1924 and 1926 as her dissertation under Lewin. She had enrolled at the Friedrich Wilhelm University in 1922 and graduated in 1925. The paper occupies pages 1 to 85 of volume 9, published inside Lewin's series 'Untersuchungen zur Handlungs- und Affektpsychologie'.

evidence: Every figure below is read off the abridged English translation, which is the document fetched for this entry. The German original was not obtained. MacLeod's reference list places the translation at pages 300 to 314 of Ellis's source book of Gestalt psychology, published in 1938. It reports 164 individually tested participants, described as students, teachers and children, plus two group experiments of 47 adults and 45 children. Each participant was given 18 to 22 short tasks, half of them stopped before completion. The translation names constructing a cardboard box, modelling clay figures, puzzles and arithmetic; MacLeod, reading the German, adds thread winding, paper folding, multiplication, drawing a vase and counting backwards. Zeigarnik timed each interruption for the moment the participant was most engrossed. Among the first 32 participants, recall favoured the interrupted tasks at IR/CR = 1.9, with 26 recalling interrupted tasks best, 3 level and 3 recalling completed tasks best. Of the 22 tasks used, 17 were better recalled when interrupted. A repeat with 15 new participants and a new task set gave 2.0, and the two group experiments gave 1.9 for adults and 2.1 for children. Interrupting tasks and then allowing them to be resumed wiped out the advantage, which she read as ruling out the shock of interruption, and telling participants that a task would or would not be resumed left ratios of 1.7 and 1.8. Her quantitative results count only the tasks named before a participant's first hesitation, which she treated as spontaneous recall. MacLeod cites page 13 of the German for her statement that pre-hesitation and total recall did not differ, and that sentence is not in the translation.

replication.headline: A 2025 meta-analysis of 38 publications puts recall of interrupted against completed tasks at a ratio of 0.99, against 1.61 for Zeigarnik's own study on that measure.
replication.detail: Ghibellini and Meier searched PsycInfo and PSYINDEX on 14 September 2023, screened 1,349 records after removing duplicates and included 59 publications, 38 of them on the Zeigarnik effect. The standard measure is the ratio of mean recall of interrupted tasks to mean recall of completed tasks. It came out at 0.99 across those 38 publications, and stayed at 0.99 with Zeigarnik's own study removed. Their Table 1 recomputes her study at 1.61 on that measure, with interrupted tasks at 61.25% of everything recalled. Her preferred measure, the mean of each participant's IR/CR, gave 1.13 across the 7 publications reporting it, and 1.09 with her own value taken out, against the 1.9 she published. Across 13 publications excluding hers, interrupted tasks made up 49.16% of everything recalled. The mid-century record runs both ways. Marrow's 1938 study of 30 participants on 20 paper-and-pencil tasks gave IR/CR = 1.77, with 25 participants recalling interrupted tasks better, 3 level and 2 recalling completed tasks better, while Schlote's 1930 results did not support her. Ghibellini and Meier point to Van Bergen's 1968 dissertation, published by North-Holland, as the in-depth replication of the original. She began in 1961, tested 34 participants at her home and found IR/CR = 0.88, with 20 recalling completed tasks better, 9 interrupted and 5 level. A close copy of Marrow's study gave 0.88 again, and a further run with a new experimenter and 25 participants reproduced the null. Seven experiments in, she reported that none of them had verified the effect, and her review of 44 replication attempts said that fewer than half had found it. MacLeod's recount of those same 44 papers puts the figure below a third.

study.cite: Ghibellini, R., & Meier, B. (2025). Interruption, recall and resumption: a meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 12(1), 962.

limits: The meta-analysis publishes weighted point values. No confidence interval and no test for publication bias appears anywhere in its text or in either of its two tables, so the pooled ratios carry no stated precision. Its one standardised effect size, Cohen's dz = 0.15, rests on the 8 publications that reported enough per-participant data, and it points weakly in the effect's favour. The measures disagree, and that disagreement is the honest state of the evidence. The moderator picture is not empty either. Grouping 16 publications by experimental atmosphere gave 1.07 in relaxed conditions, 0.96 in neutral ones and 0.88 in achievement conditions. The authors argue that the experimenter authority and task involvement of Zeigarnik's era are rare in modern samples, which they attribute in part to phone notifications, email and multitasking. Achievement motivation produced no pattern across 7 publications: 1.00 for high, 0.92 for moderate, 0.96 for low. Van Bergen's dissertation could not be obtained for this entry, so its figures are quoted as MacLeod reports them. What did survive the same meta-analysis is the neighbouring Ovsiankina effect, the tendency to go back to an interrupted task, at a weighted resumption rate of 67.00% across 21 publications, and 66.79% with Ovsiankina's own study removed.
misreadings: The waiter is an anecdote about Lewin, not a study. Boring's 1957 telling, on page 734, has a Berlin waiter recall the bill until it is paid and then forget it; MacKinnon, who was at the table, remembered the waiter reciting what each person had ordered, in a version Marrow printed in 1969. Zeigarnik tested students, teachers and children on paper and clay, and no waiter appears in the translation of her paper. Resumption is the second confusion: Ovsiankina's finding that people return to interrupted tasks holds up, and it is not evidence that they remember them better. A third strand is offered as modern support and measures something else. Wendsche, Weigelt and Syrek's 2026 meta-analysis found unfinished work tasks related to work-related thoughts during off-job time. The correlation was rho = .382 between persons across 17 studies of 2,473 people, and rho = .247 within persons across 14 studies of 12,129. That is rumination about pending work, not recall of interrupted laboratory tasks. Ongchoco, Wong and Scholl reported a visual Zeigarnik effect in 2026, four experiments with 120 observers who reproduced probe positions more precisely when a path stopped short of its end point. That is a claim about perception rather than about memory for tasks. The highest ratio in the meta-analysis's own table is Baddeley's 1.96, from 1963. It came from anagrams whose solutions were shown after 60 seconds, which ends the intention rather than leaving it open, and Baddeley called his own result 'Zeigarnik-like'. Ghibellini and Meier reran that design in 2024 with more than 1,000 adults. Unsolved anagrams were better recalled than solved ones, and the advantage sat with people high in hope of success rather than with persisting tension.
